I think it's fair to say they're raising the bar for post game content. My favorite devs are those that release a game and then spend the next few months working on improvements and adding content. I think that Blizzard did this with Diablo 3 and Respawn did this with Titanfall. It's encouraging to see devs acknowledged for going the extra mile and realizing that a game can be an ongoing experience in a non-subscription manner.

They're also abusing the steam system by labeling things that most games consider "normal updates" as "free DLC". And breaking their "free updates" into as small of pieces as they can so they stay on the front page of new releases.

Every week, like clockwork, they release a new re-skinned crossbow, or a new sword, or a 2 minute long "bonus quest", or a slightly tweak to one character's hairstyle. Just for example of what they've already done.

It's not really working for free if you do it right. Every game is the most powerful advertizing a sequel could ever get. DLC gives replay value, and it does it over a time scale that keeps the first game in people's minds until closer to the release of the sequel.

That said, full-on expansions are a different story, essentially another game on the same engine, and I don't really take issue to paying again for something the size of a typical C&C expansion.

Free DLC is good publicity, it will bring your game back into the sights of people who didn't buy it at launch.

You know what we used to call free DLC? An update.

I'm not sure large free content patches were any more common in the past than they are now. Usually you'd pay for an expansion.

There seems to be a false idea that gaming used to be cheaper and developers and publishers used to be more consumer friendly in the past.

Back in the days of the arcade gamers were always nickle and dimed, literally

Older cash shop MMO's frequently had to add new content, raise level caps in order to keep their player base interested. The concept of adding new content at no cost to the consumer isn't unheard of in the subscription MMO universe either, where new dungeons with increasingly better gear are an expected part of the release cycle.

The developer put the time and money into their product with the hope that an update might renew interest and sell some units, or in the longer term, breed a community that might support a future installment in the game. Calling it free DLC is half threat, half pride in my opinion. "Look at this awesome thing I made (to encourage unit sales). I could have charged you for this, but I'm such a nice guy..."

If you're paying a subscription or the game lives off of a cash shop, "free dlc" is irrelevant.

If you're paying a subscription, you are paying monthly and will go elsewhere if there is no extra content.

If the game is free to play than the content update is to keep you playing and using the cash shop, and not going to a game which is better supported.
And if you're getting the free content because the developer felt that it would be a positive investment with a return in the form of future purchases...?

I would call that free dlc / free content, just like we get now from the Witcher 3, or from Larian with their upcoming huge free expansion to Divinity: Original Sin, or the consistent free content of Cities: Skylines.

If anything free content is more common now than it used to be, because it used to cost more to not only give free content (logistically, a lot of content would have to be shipped on expansion CDs) but also to make people aware of free content. magazines cost money to get featured on them, word of mouth was not nearly as powerful as it is now, and in most games the free content is given automatically, through the power of the internet.

Are they still not going to release modding tools even though they promised?

If not, then same old big bark, no bite.

I think this should be a nuanced issue. If we're talking about DLC like "two new missions and a fancy new dress" or Oblivions infamous "horse armor", then yes, I do believe these content patches (for that's what they are) should be free to the user.

If, on the other hand, we are talking about proper expansion sized-content (say, The Frozen Throne for Warcraft 3) with dozens of new missions, new gameplay content, et cetera, I'm happy to pay up if the base game was also worth my money.

I don't mind free stuff, but I also get that game development is expensive and that if it doesn't turn a profit then I don't get new games. I'm willing to fork over a little bit for a DLC or micropayments in a game if it keeps Bioware afloat.

Downvotes were originally introduced as a way to help control spam posts and to help bad content stay at the bottom so that good content can rise to the top. In theory this is a good feature but in practice it doesn't work quite as well.

Downvotes are used to disagree with posts and in extreme cases to censor posts.

Right now I have a controversial comment that has 4 upvotes and like 13 downvotes. Some may care about their internet points, but I don't. My issue is that now my post that has 4 upvotes is hidden when the top comment has 9 and the 2nd comment has 3. Both of those comments state almost the exact same thought word for word. My comment goes against the grain and thus hidden in the circle jerk even though I have more people who like my post than the 2nd most upvoted comment because my comment is controversial.

There's a few issues with this system. The one I care most about is that controversial comments lead to discussion.

When everyone says something is bad or something is good there is no discussion and a circlejerk happens. When opposite viewpoints try to contribute they are hidden. This means that anyone who is lurking only gets the popular opinion.

I propose that Upvotes and Downvotes are treated like agree and disagree buttons. The more people who like a post, the higher it rises. The people who don't like a post can still down vote and show that they disagree so that a lurker can see that a highly upvoted post is still controversial, but now that a controversial post is towards the top and it sparks discussion instead of being hidden.
